rebelrebel draws maps on [MapLibre](https://maplibre.org) from data that stay in DuckDB: a parquet file, a lazy
table, a data frame or an sf object. A map is built with the pipe, a layer at a time, and every map below is live:
pan it, zoom it, click a point.

## A first map

The example data are the positions of four vessels on the Icelandic groundfish survey in March 2019, one row a
position, with whether a tow was on.

```{r}
library(rebelrebel)
positions <- rr_example("trawlsurvey")
positions |> rr_point(colour = behaviour)
```

`colour` takes a column written bare. Its values get a colour each and a legend; the map opens on the rows' extent.

## Layers with the pipe

`rr_map()` starts a map from data, and each layer function adds a layer over the ones before. Here a line per vessel
in the order of time, and the positions over it: two columns to colour by (the first shown; the other is a choice in
the page), and a click that shows the row.

```{r}
rr_map(positions) |>
  rr_path(group = vid, time = time, name = "Tracks") |>
  rr_point(
    colour = c(behaviour, speed),
    popup = c(vid, time, speed, behaviour),
    name = "Positions"
  )
```

`rr_map()` with no data starts a map whose layers bring their own. The survey's tows are lines, one a row:

```{r}
#| out-height: 400px
rr_map() |>
  rr_line(rr_example("trawlsurveytows"), name = "Tows") |>
  rr_point(positions, colour = behaviour, name = "Positions",
           visible = FALSE)
```

`visible = FALSE` leaves a layer off when the page opens; its box in the sidebar turns it on.

## In MapLibre's own terms

Every layer function takes MapLibre's paint and layout properties by their own names, in quotes, for what its own
arguments do not reach; and `id`, the name a page's address and a script know the layer by. Here the positions faster
than 12 knots get a ring of a fixed size over the others:

```{r}
fast <- dplyr::filter(positions, speed > 12)
rr_map(positions) |>
  rr_point(colour = behaviour, name = "Positions") |>
  rr_point(fast, colour = "#00a5c8", id = "fast", name = "Over 12 knots",
           "circle-color" = "rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)", "circle-radius" = 7,
           "circle-stroke-color" = "#00a5c8", "circle-stroke-width" = 2)
```

## A layer of your own

What the layer functions do not draw, an `rr_layer()` does: elevations as colours and relief, contours, tiles of your
own. `rr_add_layer()` puts one into the pipe, in a box of the sidebar of its own. Here the depth of the Danish waters
in colour, made into tiles from a grid of elevations by `rr_tiles_dem()`, under the harbours:

```{r}
depth <- rr_layer(
  "depth", "dem", label = "Depth",
  tiles = rr_tiles_dem(rr_example("dansk_relief"), maxzoom = 6),
  style = list(list(id = "depth-colour", type = "color-relief")),
  colour = list(palette = "seabed", opacity = 75)
)
rr_map(view = list(bounds = c(2.5, 54.5, 13, 58.5))) |>
  rr_add_layer(depth, section = "Sea floor") |>
  rr_polygon(rr_example("dansk_harbours"), name = "Harbours")
```

The harbours reach from Greenland to the Black Sea, so `view` opens the map on the grid's box. Elevations and
contours go under the base map's place names, whatever their order in the pipe; the box *Depth* has the colours'
controls.

## Showing and sharing

- **In R**, printing a map serves it on this computer and opens it in RStudio's Viewer or a browser.
- **In a document** (Quarto, R Markdown, a pkgdown article like this one), a printed map is drawn live in the page.
- **As a folder**, `rr_bundle(map, "my-map")` writes the map with its data, to open with a double click on any
  computer, with no R and no server.
